newsitem.title: MEXICO: Tensions build as Mexico rebel truce nears end.
newsitem.headline: Tensions build as Mexico rebel truce nears end.

text.p: Fear has returned to this small town in guerrilla country as the Mexican army prepares for Sunday's end of a unilateral truce called by the rebel Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR).
The Guerrero state governor's pleas to extend the truce and open negotiations have been ignored by both guerrillas and government, with neither side appearing willing to talk.

The one-month respite, called so local elections could be carried out unimpeded earlier this month, gave the 11,000 people of Coyuca de Benitez a chance to remember what life was like before the EPR made its debut appearance on June 28.

With the truce set to expire at 8:30 p.m. Sunday (0230 GMT Monday), truckloads of army soldiers patrolled with greater frequency, and frightened citizens rarely left their homes at night, one elected local official told Reuters.
"Once again the people are fearful to walk around freely in the streets," Carmelo Garcia Agustiano said from his office just off a noisy corridor at City Hall.
"They have implemented military roadblocks, they are demanding that people carry their voter identification cards, asking questions," he said, charging army intimidation of the local population.

One sign of the military build-up was the sudden presence of elite troops with black berets and painted faces patrolling the rural outskirts of Coyuca in armoured vehicles. Military helicopters and planes regularly buzz overhead.
Coyuca de Benitez is a staggeringly poor town an hour's drive from the world-famous Pacific beach resort of Acapulco.

Like much of rural Guerrero state, it is fertile ground for armed revolt. Campesinos eke out a living with a machete, hacking down coconuts or growing corn or beans. A very few lucky ones from towns land jobs at Acapulco's luxury hotels.
"These towns are living in extreme poverty," Garcia said. "We have health clinics but no medicine, no doctors. We have schools but no teachers, or vice-versa."

On June 28, 1995, state government police gunned down 17 peasants on their way to a leftist protest in Coyuca, only to be caught on videotape planting guns in the hands of the dead in a crude attempt to feign self-defence.
Subsequent public outrage forced the governor of Guerrero state Ruben Figueroa to resign in disgrace.

During a recent hunger strike to profess their innocence, the state policemen accused of the massacre claimed that the protesters were really a nascent EPR, claiming they just hadn't donned their masks and olive green fatigues yet.

On June 28, at a ceremony marking the anniversary of the massacre, the EPR introduced itself to Mexico, unveiling their shiny automatic weapons, but not their faces, stunning a nation on the brink of peace with the unrelated Zapatista guerrillas in southern Chiapas state.
The EPR launched a series of minor ambushes and one major operation attacking military targets in five states on Aug. 28-30 that left 17 people dead, according to the government.

Angel Aguirre Rivero, the replacement governor of Guerrero and a member of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), has defied federal authorities by calling for negotiations with the EPR while the central government insist on crushing the group, which it labels as "terrorists."
"The governor of the state of Guerrero is more than willing to sit down and dialogue with the members of the EPR," Aguirre told reporters last week.
Aguirre later was rebuked by Jose Natividad Gonzalez Parras, a top Interior Ministry official, who told reporters the only government contact with the EPR would be, "in the prosecution of justice."
